analysis.one_liner: Lets the FTC and state attorneys general police internet and broadband companies for privacy and data-security abuses.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and one of its subcommittees in May 2017 and sat there until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for broadband providers and internet companies to use unfair or deceptive practices involving privacy or data security. It would let the Federal Trade Commission write rules to enforce that, extend FTC enforcement to phone and cable companies that are currently exempt, and let state attorneys general sue violators in federal court on behalf of their residents. It never advanced past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Broadband and internet users, who would gain a federal privacy and data-security standard enforced by the FTC and state attorneys general, including against cable and phone companies currently exempt from FTC oversight.

how_it_helps.text: It makes it unlawful for broadband providers and edge providers (companies offering content, apps, services, or devices over the internet) to engage in unfair or deceptive acts or practices relating to privacy or data security.
It directs the FTC to enforce the prohibition with the full powers of the Federal Trade Commission Act, and lets the FTC write rules to carry out the standard after consulting the FCC.

It removes two enforcement gaps: the FTC would be able to pursue common carriers regulated under the Communications Act of 1934, which are currently exempt from FTC enforcement, and nonprofit organizations, which are currently subject to FTC enforcement only in narrow circumstances.
It gives state attorneys general the power to sue violators in federal court on behalf of their states' residents, adding a second layer of enforcement.

analysis.who_pays: Broadband providers, internet content and service companies, device makers, and covered nonprofits, through compliance costs and exposure to FTC and state enforcement actions.

drawbacks.text: The FTC's authority to write rules under a broad 'unfair' standard gives regulators wide discretion, which would mean compliance costs for internet companies of every size, including small services and device makers, not just the largest firms.

State attorneys general could bring overlapping federal suits, and while the FTC can intervene and a state must pause a suit over a defendant already named in an FTC action, companies would face enforcement from multiple fronts at once.

The bill builds on the FTC's consumer-protection statute rather than the FCC's telecom authority, so broadband privacy would be policed case-by-case as deception or unfairness rather than through bright-line disclosure or consent rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and sizable: it would close the main enforcement gap that lets cable and phone companies handle subscribers' browsing data outside FTC oversight, and would give users a national privacy and data-security backstop plus state-level enforcement. The costs are the usual ones for a consumer-protection standard — compliance burdens that fall hardest on small internet businesses and some duplicative multi-agency litigation — but they are the costs any enforceable privacy rule carries.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, then to a subcommittee the next day, and neither ever took it up before the two-year Congress expired.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerry McNerney (D-CA) introduced the bill on May 4, 2017, joined by five colleagues as original cosponsors: Reps. DeGette, Engel, Rush, Khanna, and Takano.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce; on May 5, 2017, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Digital Commerce and Consumer Protection.
Seven members cosponsored the bill, all Democrats; no Republican cosponsored it.
That was the last action ever taken: the bill received no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband providers and internet companies keep their existing exemptions and the fragmented privacy rules, so the industries that would have faced FTC and state enforcement avoided it, and users remain without the federal standard the bill offered.

industries.note: These companies are currently exempt from FTC enforcement because they are regulated as common carriers, leaving their handling of subscribers' data outside the main consumer-protection cop. The bill ends that exemption and exposes them to FTC rulemaking and state suits; that interest runs directly against users' privacy. [S3]

industries.industry: Internet content, app, and service companies
industries.note: These edge providers are already covered by the FTC's general deception authority, so the bill mainly adds a privacy-specific 'unfairness' standard, rulemaking, and state enforcement, meaning new compliance and litigation exposure while raising the bar against mishandling user data.

Devices used to access internet content and services fall under the bill's definition of edge provider, so they would face the same privacy and data-security enforcement as software and service companies.

Nonprofits not organized for profit are currently outside FTC jurisdiction except in narrow cases; the bill makes them subject to the same privacy and data-security prohibition, a modest compliance cost in exchange for covering a currently unregulated channel for consumer data.
